issues.legal_issue: Procedural instructions governing compulsory-retirement reviews under a rule that contains no review criteria are binding on the government when they protect the employee from prejudicial action.
material_facts: The governing retirement rule contained no guidelines, directions, or criteria for deciding whether an officer should be compulsorily retired.
The government had issued instructions prescribing a procedure to promote uniformity and equitable treatment in such reviews.
The officer’s retirement followed a review process that the Court found inconsistent with those instructions.
issues.conclusion: The instructions filled gaps in the rule, formed part of the conditions of service, and could not be violated to the employee’s prejudice.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 16(3) of the All India Services (Death-cum-Retirement Benefits) Rules, 1958 contained no review criteria. The procedural instructions supplied an essential safeguard, were embedded in the conditions of service, and bound the government. The Court applied Santram Sharma v. State of Rajasthan and Union of India v. K. P. Joseph.

rule.if: compulsory_retirement_review_case and rule_lacks_review_criteria and government_issued_review_procedure and procedure_was_departed_from_to_employee_prejudice

predicates.compulsory_retirement_review_case: The government considered whether to compulsorily retire a public employee.
predicates.rule_lacks_review_criteria: The rule governing the review supplied no guidelines or criteria for deciding whether the employee should be retired.
predicates.government_issued_review_procedure: The government issued procedural instructions to guide and standardize the review.
predicates.procedure_was_departed_from_to_employee_: The government departed from the instructed procedure in a way that disadvantaged the employee.

issues.definition: When a compulsory-retirement rule lacks review criteria, government-issued review procedures bind the government if departing from them prejudices the employee.

issues.legal_issue: After a favorable review has been accepted by the state and the central government has taken no adverse decision, the employee’s case cannot ordinarily be reassessed on the same material before the next review stage unless exceptional circumstances arise.
material_facts: A first review committee recommended that the officer continue in service, and the state government accepted that recommendation.
After seeking the state government’s views, the central government did not decide to take adverse action against the officer.
A second committee reconsidered the officer on the same materials before the next scheduled review stage and recommended compulsory retirement.
No exceptional circumstances or fresh material justified reopening the review.
issues.conclusion: The second committee could not reassess the officer on the same materials in the ordinary course, and the retirement order based on its recommendation could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 16(3) of the All India Services (Death-cum-Retirement Benefits) Rules, 1958, read with the binding procedural instructions, ordinarily permits review at the prescribed stages and does not warrant a second review on the same material after a favorable review unless exceptional circumstances emerge or the next review stage arrives. A newly disclosed concern about integrity may constitute an exceptional circumstance.

rule.if: compulsory_retirement_review_case and first_review_recommended_continuance and state_accepted_continuance and central_government_took_no_adverse_decision and second_review_used_same_materials and second_review_preceded_next_stage and no_exceptional_circumstances

predicates.compulsory_retirement_review_case: The government considered whether to compulsorily retire a public employee.
predicates.first_review_recommended_continuance: The first review committee recommended that the employee remain in service.
predicates.state_accepted_continuance: The state government accepted the recommendation that the employee remain in service.
predicates.central_government_took_no_adverse_decis: After receiving or considering the state’s position, the central government did not decide to take adverse action against the employee.
predicates.second_review_used_same_materials: A later review committee reassessed the employee using the same material considered in the first review.
predicates.second_review_preceded_next_stage: The later review occurred before the next prescribed review stage.
predicates.no_exceptional_circumstances: No exceptional circumstance, such as newly arising weighty material, justified reopening the case.

issues.definition: A retirement order based on a second review is invalid when a favorable first review was accepted, the central government took no adverse decision, the second review reused the same material before the next stage, and no exceptional circumstance arose.

issues.legal_issue: A bona fide, non-stigmatic compulsory-retirement order under the service rules is not a punitive dismissal or removal.
material_facts: The officer was compulsorily retired under the service rule after reaching the relevant service threshold.
The order was not a disciplinary punishment and did not cast a stigma on the officer.
The officer did not allege mala fides before the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: Compulsory retirement of this kind is not equivalent to dismissal or removal by way of punishment, although an arbitrary or mala fide order may be challenged.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rule 16(2) and (3) of the All India Services (Death-cum-Retirement Benefits) Rules, 1958, an employee who has reached the specified service threshold cannot insist on continued service, and the government has a corresponding power to retire the employee in the public interest. The Court considered Articles 309, 310 and 311 of the Constitution and distinguished compulsory retirement from punitive dismissal or removal; it also referred to State of Orissa v. Bidyabhushan Mahapatra on the effect of surviving grounds in a punitive order.

rule.if: compulsory_retirement_case and service_threshold_reached and order_is_bona_fide and order_casts_no_stigma and earned_benefits_are_not_forfeited

predicates.compulsory_retirement_case: The government ended an employee’s service by compulsory retirement under a service rule.
predicates.service_threshold_reached: The employee had reached the service period or age at which the rule permitted compulsory retirement.
predicates.order_is_bona_fide: The government made the retirement decision honestly and not for an improper purpose.
predicates.order_casts_no_stigma: The retirement order does not stigmatize the employee.
predicates.earned_benefits_are_not_forfeited: The retirement does not take away benefits the employee already earned through service.

issues.definition: When an employee has reached the relevant service threshold and a bona fide compulsory-retirement order neither stigmatizes the employee nor forfeits earned benefits, the retirement is not punitive.

issues.legal_issue: The preventive-detention test for invalidating an order because one of several grounds is irrelevant or nonexistent does not govern a non-stigmatic compulsory-retirement order.
material_facts: The order under review was one of compulsory retirement, not preventive detention or disciplinary dismissal.
One consideration relied on in support of retirement concerned strictures that had been expunged, but the retirement order rested on several grounds.
The order did not impose a stigma, and the officer had no continuing right to insist on retention in service after reaching the applicable threshold.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not invalidate the compulsory-retirement order by applying the preventive-detention test to the ground that had ceased to exist; that analogy did not apply to this kind of order.
issues.legal_principle: The preventive-detention rule concerning effective representation protects the constitutional right to individual liberty and does not apply to a non-stigmatic compulsory-retirement order under Rule 16(3), which is not a penal order. The Court referred to State of Orissa v. Bidyabhushan Mahapatra, where a punitive dismissal was not invalidated when surviving findings established grave misconduct despite other grounds failing.

predicates.compulsory_retirement_challenge: A court is reviewing an order that compulsorily retired a public employee.
predicates.order_casts_no_stigma: The retirement order does not stigmatize the employee.
predicates.employee_has_no_right_to_insist_on_conti: Under the applicable service conditions, the employee had no right to demand continued service after reaching the relevant threshold.

issues.definition: The preventive-detention ground test does not apply when a court reviews a non-stigmatic compulsory-retirement order against an employee who cannot insist on continued service.
